analysis.one_liner: Phases out private prisons, reinstates federal parole, and caps prison phone and money-transfer fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended federal, state, and local contracts with private prison companies within about two years, requiring governments to run their own prisons and jails with public employees. It would have reinstated parole for federal prisoners sentenced after the start of 2017, capped what companies can charge inmates' families for phone calls and money transfers, and eliminated the requirement that immigration authorities keep at least 34,000 detention beds filled. It also banned family detention, created alternatives to detention for immigrant families, and required regular independent inspections of all detention facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of prisoners and immigration detainees, who currently pay high per-minute phone rates and money-transfer fees; federal prisoners, who would regain a chance at parole; immigrant families facing detention; and inmates held in privately operated facilities, who would come under direct government operation with mandated inspections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prisoners' families, inmates, and detained immigrants

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred private companies from holding federal prisoners or detainees: within two years, every facility housing adult federal prisoners and detainees would be under direct government control, run by government employees, with a one-year waiver if the Attorney General determined compliance was not possible.
It required state and local governments to do the same for their own prisons and jails, with the same one-year waiver option.
It reinstated federal parole, abolished by the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984, for prisoners sentenced on or after January 1, 2017, making most eligible after serving a third of their sentence.

It directed the FCC to cap prison phone call rates and connection charges, require collect and debit call options, restrict the commissions phone companies pay to jails, and allow more than one provider so inmates have a choice.

It required the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to set standards ensuring fees for money transfers into prisons and detention facilities are reasonable and proportional to the service's actual cost.

It struck the requirement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement maintain at least 34,000 detention beds, replaced detention capacity with actual need, established nationwide alternatives-to-detention programs, banned family detention, and prohibited separating families apprehended together.
It required annual government inspections and independent audits of all detention facilities, with financial penalties for failing standards and contract termination for repeat violators.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies would lose federal and state contracts; inmate phone and money-transfer companies would lose their fee structures; and jails that count on phone commissions as revenue would lose that income. Taxpayers could face transition costs as governments built capacity to run facilities directly, and some federal prisoners would serve shorter terms under restored parole.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison, phone, and money-transfer companies

drawbacks.text: Restored parole eligibility after serving a third of a sentence, and mandatory release at two-thirds for longer sentences, would mean earlier release for some federal prisoners, which critics of parole expansion see as a public-safety risk.

The two-year timeline for governments to take over every prison and jail was tight enough that the bill itself included a waiver if the Attorney General determined compliance was impossible, and states could have faced real costs converting contract facilities to public operation.
The bill preempted state and local rules on inmate phone commissions, overriding decisions local officials had made about their own jail revenues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are concrete and focused on people with little economic power: families paying phone and transfer fees, inmates in private facilities, and detained families. The main costs fall on a small set of companies profiting from incarceration, plus transition costs for governments and a genuine public-safety tradeoff in earlier parole releases. The design is workable — the waivers acknowledge the transition burden — but the tight timeline would have been a real implementation challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then three subcommittees in the fall of 2015, and no committee ever held a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on September 17, 2015, with 19 original cosponsors joining him at introduction.

The bill was referred to four committees at once — Judiciary, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, and Homeland Security — meaning no single committee controlled it and each could have claimed jurisdiction.
In the following weeks it was referred to subcommittees on Communications and Technology, Border and Maritime Security, and Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
After those referrals, the action history shows no further activity: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point in the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017.
All 30 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced in a Congress where Republicans held the House majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison companies, inmate phone providers, and money-transfer companies kept their contracts and fee structures untouched for another two years, and the 34,000 detention bed requirement remained in place.

industries.industry: Private prison and detention facility operators
industries.note: The bill would have ended all federal, state, and local contracts with private prison companies within about two years, removing their core revenue from housing federal inmates and ICE detainees. Companies running detention centers would also have faced independent audits and financial penalties for substandard conditions.

industries.industry: Inmate phone and video service providers
industries.note: The FCC would have been required to cap per-minute rates and connection fees, limit or ban the commissions these companies pay to jails, and bar ancillary fees — directly cutting a business model built on high rates charged to inmates' families.

industries.industry: Money transfer providers serving correctional facilities
industries.note: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau standards would force fees for sending money to inmates and detainees to be reasonable and proportional to actual cost, constraining what these companies can charge.

industries.industry: State and local correctional agencies that collect phone commissions
industries.note: Jails and corrections departments receive commission payments from phone providers based on inmate call revenue; the bill would have restricted or prohibited those payments, though federal rules would override their state and local arrangements either way.

Government employees would perform core correctional services at all prisons and detention centers, and a reestablished federal parole system would require staffing the Parole Commission and supervision work.
